Speaking at the opening of the 59th session of Puntland’s parliament in Garowe on Saturday, Deni said his administration would not participate in the federal government-led electoral process, deepening the standoff over Somalia’s electoral framework. He called on Somalis to engage in dialogue and reach a political understanding on the country’s direction, stressing the need for an inclusive settlement that accounts for all stakeholders’ positions. “The Puntland government calls on all different parts of Somalia to come together urgently, to save Somali statehood,” Deni said. He also urged the international community to closely monitor Somalia’s political situation and support a consultative process to address the divisions. The Puntland leader accused President Mohamud of refusing to hold an agreed election and of obstructing talks on the electoral process. His remarks come as the federal government maintains that presidential elections will be held on May 15, 2027, with parliamentary elections set for April 15 of the same year. A Fractured Political Landscape Deni’s warning is the latest escalation in a prolonged dispute that has seen Puntland, Jubaland, and the opposition Somali Future Council reject the federal government’s electoral timetable and constitutional amendments. The opposition coalition has accused President Mohamud of taking unilateral decisions that threaten national unity and the federal system. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the political crisis , former Puntland President Abdirahman Mohamed Faroole has declared that there is “no legitimate government in Mogadishu,” reflecting the depth of the rift between Garowe and the federal capital. Puntland has formally rejected the constitutional amendments, arguing that they undermine the federal system and concentrate excessive power in the hands of the federal presidency, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Puntland’s rejection . The political confrontation has been compounded by practical tensions. The federal government’s enforcement of the National ID requirement for domestic travel has created disruptions for Puntland residents, as NIRA does not operate registration offices in the region. Puntland has rejected the federal ID system, with Deni signing a decree in 2025 creating the Puntland Identification Authority to issue cards independently, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the ID dispute . Hassan Sheikh Meets Puntland Elder Over Nugaal Killings Against this backdrop of political confrontation, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud met with Puntland traditional leader Islaan Ciise Islaan Mohamed at the Presidential Palace, with discussions reportedly focusing on the deaths of 13 people along the Garmaal and Jiifle coastal areas in the Nugaal region. According to information obtained about the meeting, Islaan Ciise urged the federal government to pursue accountability, ensure justice for the victims, and protect the rights of their bereaved families. The incident has heightened concerns over civilian safety along Puntland’s coastline, particularly among fishing communities whose livelihoods depend on access to the sea. Puntland’s administration has previously said the victims were civilian fishermen and accused Turkish forces of carrying out an attack that killed people not involved in fighting. The federal government has offered a different account, with State Minister for Defence Omar Ali Abdi stating that the government was aware of military operations along the coast and that any operation against piracy would legally require federal authorization. The circumstances surrounding the strike remain contested. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the airstrikes controversy , Turkey has stated it has no information regarding airstrikes off the Puntland coast that killed nine people, amid growing controversy over attacks that reportedly targeted a mix of fishermen and individuals suspected of being part of pirate networks. Puntland later called for an independent international investigation into the strikes, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the demand . Puntland President Deni has addressed the escalating security situation, expressing dissatisfaction with how the strikes were conducted and emphasizing the need for legal accountability. “We are not satisfied with how things happened, and we are deeply concerned. If someone commits a crime, we do not need to take extrajudicial action; crime has a legal process to follow,” Deni stated. Critical Note Deni’s call for urgent dialogue and his decision to boycott the federal electoral process are not isolated gestures. They represent a calculated strategy by Puntland to position itself as the principal alternative center of political authority in Somalia, at a moment when the federal government’s legitimacy is contested by multiple stakeholders. The meeting between President Mohamud and Islaan Ciise is a recognition that the Nugaal killings have created a humanitarian and political crisis that cannot be ignored. But a single meeting with a traditional elder does not resolve the underlying questions about accountability, civilian protection, and the role of foreign military operations in Puntland’s territory. The families of the victims have been promised justice. Whether they receive it will depend on whether the federal government is willing to investigate an operation that Puntland believes was conducted by its Turkish partners. The two developments, Deni’s political offensive and the Nugaal killings, are connected by more than timing. They both expose the fragility of the federal compact and the extent to which Puntland’s relationship with Mogadishu has deteriorated. Deni’s warning that Somali statehood is at risk is not hyperbole. It is a description of a political landscape in which the federal government and its most powerful regional ally are moving in opposite directions, with no agreed framework for resolving their differences. The call for urgent talks is necessary. But talks require willing partners, and the gap between Garowe and Mogadishu has never been wider. Posted by: Horseed Staff Madaxweynaha Dowladda Puntland Siciid Cabdullaahi Deni, oo khudbad ka jeediyey munaasabadda furitaanka kal-fadhiga 59aad ee barlamaanka… 25 October, 2026 Share Tweet Madaxweynaha Dowladda Puntland Siciid Cabdullaahi Deni, oo khudbad ka jeediyey munaasabadda furitaanka kal-fadhiga 59aad ee barlamaanka ayaa si adag uga hadlay xaaladda siyaasadeed ee Soomaaliya, khilaafka doorashooyinka, waxka-beddelka dastuurka iyo mowqifka Puntland ee ku aaddan dhismaha dowladnimada Soomaaliyeed. Siciid Cabdullaahi Deni, ayaa sheegay in Soomaaliya ay gashay xaalad uu ku tilmaamay mid halis ku ah dowladnimada dalka, isaga oo ku eedeeyay dowladda Federaalka inay ka leexatay heshiisyadii lagu dhisay nidaamka federaalka, isagoo xusay in Puntland ay muddo dheer dadaal ugu jirtay dhismaha dowlad Soomaaliyeed oo federaal ah, taas oo uu sheegay in ujeeddadeedu ahayd in dalka laga hirgeliyo xasillooni iyo nidaam dowladeed oo dhammaystiran. “Dowladda Puntland waxay marwalba u taagan tahay dhismaha dowladnimo Soomaaliyeed oo federal ah wadadaas oo aan ku bixinay dedaal nooc kasta ah si loo gaaro xasilooni iyo nidaamo dowladnimo oo dhammaystiran, waxaan aad uga xumahay in maanta dalku uu galay xaalad halis ku ah dowladnimada Soomaaliyeed ee muddada dheer laga soo shaqaynayey”, Ayuu yiri Madaxweynaha Dowladda Puntland Siciid Cabdullaahi Deni. Madaxweynaha Puntland ayaa sheegay in meesha laga saaray heshiisyadii siyaasadeed ee ay Soomaalidu hore ugu heshiisay, oo uu ku jiro Dastuurka Kumeelgaarka ah ee Soomaaliya, wuxuuna Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud ku eedeeyay inuu diiday qabashada doorasho heshiis lagu yahay, isla markaana uu caqabad ku noqday wadahadallada lagu xallin lahaa khilaafaadka siyaasadeed ee dalka, awooddii dowladnimadana lagu dhibaataynayo bulshada Soomaaliyeed. “Waxaa meesha ka baxay waxkasta oo heshiis lagu ahaa oo uu ugu dambeeyey dastuurkii kumeel gaarka ahaa ee 20212, Madaxweynaha waqtigiisu dhammaaday Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud, wuxuu diidey inuu dalka ka qabto doorasho heshiis lagu wada yahay isagoo markasta ka shaqaynayey inuu fashiliyo wadahadal-kasta, xaaladda dalku waxay gaartey in Mas’uuliyiintii u soo shaqeeyey dalka lagu weeraro drones, in xasilooni darro laga abuuro deegaano deggan, in ciidamadii lagu dhisay dhaqaalaha iyo magaca Soomaaliyeed loo adeegsado burburinta dalka iyo boobka hantidada dadka iyo dalka Soomaaliyeed”, Ayuu markale yiri Madaxweynaha Puntland. Madaxweynaha Dowladda Puntland ayaa intaasi ku daray inaysan dowladda Puntland raali ka ahayn waxa uu ugu yeeray doorasho u gaar ah Villa Somalia, isagoo ugu yeeray dhammaan umadda Soomaaliyeed in laysugu yimaado shirweyne lagu badbaadinayo dowladnimada Somalia, isagoo shaaciyey inaysan dowladda Puntland qaadan doonin go’aamo aan u qalmin shacabkeeda. “Dhammaan tallaabooyinkaasi waxaa mas’uuliyaddooda qaadaya Madaxweynaha waqtigiisu dhammaaday iyo ciddii kala shaqaysay, Dowladda Puntland waxay la wadaagaysaa umadda Soomaaliyeed iyo beesha caalamka inaysan raali ka ahayn damaca gurracan iyo nooca doorasho ee isaga u gaarka ah ee uu ku dhawaaqay Xasan Sheekh oo halis ku ah jiritaanka jamhuuriyadda Saddexaad ee Soomaaliya, sidaasi darteed Dowladda Puntland waxay ugu baaqaysaa dadka Soomaaliyeed ee turaaluhu kaga jiro dalka inay dhaqso laysugu yimaado shir lagu badbaadinayo dowladnimada Soomaaliyeed, anigoo si buuxda u garawsan dareenka shacabka Puntland waxaan idiin ballanqaadayaa inaanan qaadan doonin go’aamo aan idiin qalmin”, Ayuu yiri Madaxweynaha Dowladda Puntland. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea gained independence in 1993 and now relies on Djibouti for more than 90 percent of its import and export trade. Abiy has argued that this dependence constrains Ethiopia’s economic expansion and international competitiveness, describing maritime access as essential for the nation’s sustained advancement and self-reliance, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Abiy’s Red Sea strategy . “The main factor preventing Ethiopia from becoming self-sufficient and competing in the global economy is the absence of ports,” Abiy said in an interview with Ethiopian National Television. He has framed the issue as existential, asking publicly, “Who made the decision that caused Ethiopia to lose the Red Sea?” and insisting that the question is legal, historical, geographical, and economic, requiring a calm and thoughtful approach. The Somaliland MoU and Its Aftermath In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Somaliland, granting Addis Ababa access to a 20-kilometer coastal strip at the port of Berbera for 50 years in exchange for potential recognition of Somaliland’s independence. Somalia rejected the agreement as a “blatant violation” of its sovereignty, and the dispute escalated into a regional crisis. The Federal Government of Somalia has consistently maintained that any arrangement for Ethiopian sea access must be negotiated directly with Mogadishu and respect Somali sovereignty. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s Somaliland strategy , Addis Ababa has carefully positioned itself to move toward recognition without becoming diplomatically isolated, but the calculation remains complex. Ethiopia’s Ambassador to Israel, Tesfaye Yetayeh Anteneh, has explained the reluctance to formalize recognition by citing the risk of triggering a security collapse in Somalia. “The moment, for example, Ethiopia recognizes Somaliland, the Somali government will request Ethiopia to withdraw its troops from Somalia,” Anteneh said. “And Al-Shabaab will get a free ride to attack both Somalia and Somaliland, even a spillover effect will come also to Ethiopia.” The Ankara Declaration and Its Limits Following Turkish-mediated talks in December 2025, Somalia and Ethiopia reached a breakthrough agreement known as the Ankara Declaration. The two leaders “reaffirmed their respect and commitment to one another’s sovereignty, unity, independence and territorial integrity,” and agreed that further talks on Ethiopia’s sea access would not compromise Somalia’s sovereignty. Somalia’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Ali Omar, has said Ethiopia can secure reliable sea access through Somali territory and ports via commercial agreements that serve both countries’ interests and respect Somalia’s sovereignty. He described the Ankara Declaration as the framework governing relations between Mogadishu and Addis Ababa, and downplayed the significance of the Somaliland MoU, stating that the declaration and subsequent technical negotiations are now the current path for addressing Ethiopia’s sea access issue. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also affirmed that relations between Mogadishu and Addis Ababa remain strong, stating that his government harbors no objection to Ethiopia securing commercial sea access through joint port agreements. The Eritrea Dimension Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access has further escalated the tensions with Eritrea, which has accused Addis Ababa of waging a war agenda under the rubric of acquiring “sovereign access to the sea, through negotiations if possible and force if necessary.” Eritrea’s Information Ministry has documented a series of statements by Ethiopian officials, including military commanders, that it describes as violations of Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Abiy has publicly stated that Ethiopia does not want to go to war with Eritrea and has always sought peace, offering to travel to Asmara if his trip would yield positive results. But Eritrea’s government has characterized Ethiopia’s naval expansion and public claims to Red Sea access as a “brazen violation” of its sovereignty, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Eritrea-Ethiopia standoff . The two countries have exchanged accusations of war preparations at the United Nations Security Council, with Eritrea requesting that the council “forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea” and Ethiopia invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter to accuse Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units across the border. Russia has offered to host talks between the two neighbors, but neither side has publicly accepted the offer or indicated readiness to compromise on the core issue. What This Means for Somalia For Somalia, Abiy’s renewed emphasis on sea access is a direct concern. The Somaliland MoU, though now superseded in practice by the Ankara Declaration, demonstrated that Addis Ababa is willing to pursue alternative routes to the sea that bypass Mogadishu. The Ankara framework has eased the immediate crisis, but the underlying tension remains unresolved. Somalia’s position is clear: Ethiopia can have commercial access to Somali ports, but only through direct negotiations with the federal government and under Somali sovereignty. Whether Addis Ababa will accept that framework in the long term, or whether it will continue to explore alternatives through Somaliland or Eritrea, is the central question. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the regional standoff , Somalia has sought to maintain neutrality in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute while protecting its own sovereignty and territorial integrity. Critical Note Abiy Ahmed’s framing of sea access as an existential issue is not new. It has been a consistent theme of his government since 2023, and it resonates deeply in a country where the vast majority of trade flows through a single foreign port. The economic logic is sound: dependence on Djibouti exposes Ethiopia to tariffs, congestion, and political risk that a diversified access strategy would mitigate. But the diplomatic logic is more complicated. Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access has already destabilized its relations with Somalia and Eritrea, and the Somaliland MoU remains a sore point despite the Ankara Declaration. Abiy’s insistence that Ethiopia seeks access through peaceful means is welcome, but the region has heard such assurances before. The test is not what Ethiopia says, but what it does. For Somalia, the lesson is that the Ankara Declaration is a framework, not a solution. It buys time and creates a channel for dialogue, but it does not resolve the fundamental question of whether Ethiopia will accept a commercial arrangement under Somali sovereignty or continue to pursue alternatives. Mogadishu should use the space the Ankara framework provides to strengthen its own position, developing port infrastructure, clarifying its maritime boundaries, and building the kind of regional partnerships that make Somali sovereignty a fact rather than a claim. According to the Speaker’s Office, the event celebrated the team’s achievement in reaching the final of the regional tournament, where they ultimately fell to Uganda on penalties. But the Speaker’s message was one of pride rather than disappointment. He told the young players that they are “young heroes” who brought honor and prestige to their country and wrote a golden chapter in Somali football history that all Somalis can be proud of. Speaker Abdulkadir praised the team’s skill, courage, unity, and love for the blue flag on the field. He expressed optimism that the players will achieve greater success in regional, continental, and international competitions in the future, and that they will make Somalia proud on football pitches around the world. A Final That Deserved More The Speaker’s recognition was not merely a consolation prize. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the final , Somalia matched Uganda, the tournament’s most dominant side, for 90 minutes and created the better chances in the second half. The Ocean Stars defended with discipline, pressed intelligently in midfield, and repeatedly broke forward with purpose. In the final 10 minutes, Somalia created three clear-cut opportunities against a defense that had conceded just once in three matches. A well-worked attack in the 85th minute ended in the hands of the Ugandan goalkeeper. Another opportunity went begging in the 88th. And in the 94th minute, Mahmoud Osman, the team’s standout forward, missed a golden chance to win the match. The final whistle sent the teams to penalties, where Uganda prevailed. The loss was painful, but the performance was not. As FTL Somalia noted, “the players showed character, tactical discipline, and a refusal to be overawed by an opponent that had demolished every other team in the tournament.” A Call for Private Sector Investment The Speaker used the occasion to issue a direct appeal to large companies and financially capable businesses, urging them to make real investments in Somali sports. He argued that such investment is necessary to improve the quality of national teams, nurture youth talent, and build a better future for Somali football. The call reflects a recognition that the national team’s achievements, however impressive, have been built on limited resources. The Somali Football Federation has relied on modest budgets, diaspora support, and the commitment of volunteers. The Under-17 team’s success in reaching the continental tournament in Morocco 2027 has generated goodwill and attention, but translating that into sustained infrastructure and coaching capacity requires funding that the government alone cannot provide. The meeting was attended by the First Deputy Speaker, the Secretary General of the House of the People, ministers including the Minister of Youth and Sports, members of parliament, officials from the Somali Football Federation, and other dignitaries. A Campaign That Captured the Nation The Under-17 team’s campaign in Kigali captured the imagination of Somalis at home and abroad. The Ocean Stars drew 1-1 with defending champions Tanzania in their opener, defeated Kenya 2-0, and advanced via a toss before overcoming hosts Rwanda on penalties in the semi-final, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the semi-final . Mahmoud Osman, the team’s standout forward, was among the players celebrated by the Speaker. His equalizer against Rwanda and his goals against Kenya made him one of the tournament’s most talked-about performers, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the team’s campaign . The team’s qualification for the 2027 U-17 Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco was the primary objective, and it was achieved. The final against Uganda was an opportunity for a regional trophy, but the broader accomplishment, reaching the continental stage for the second time in four years, is a significant milestone for a country whose football infrastructure has been rebuilt from the ruins of conflict. Critical Note The Speaker’s recognition of the Under-17 team is a welcome gesture, and his call for private-sector investment in sports is a necessary one. The team’s success in Kigali was not the product of a well-funded system. It was the product of talent, determination, and the commitment of a coaching staff working with limited resources. If Somali football is to build on this achievement, it will need more than praise. It will need investment. The Speaker’s appeal to businesses is pragmatic. The government’s budget is stretched thin, and the Ministry of Youth and Sports has limited capacity to fund national teams, academies, and infrastructure. The private sector, which has prospered in Somalia’s telecommunications, banking, and logistics sectors, has the resources to make a difference. But it has not yet shown a sustained willingness to invest in sports at scale. The Speaker’s call is an invitation to change that. The deeper challenge is institutional. The Somali Football Federation has made progress in organizing regional leagues and youth tournaments, but it remains reliant on external support and volunteer energy. A national football academy, a properly funded coaching pipeline, and a domestic league that can retain talent are all necessary components of a sustainable system. The Under-17 team’s success is a proof of concept. Whether it becomes the foundation for something larger, or a fleeting moment of pride, will depend on whether the investment the Speaker called for actually materializes. According to a statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Minister Abdisalam welcomed the new ambassador and pledged the ministry’s full support for his diplomatic duties. He also congratulated the ambassador on the reopening of Oman’s embassy in Mogadishu after 36 years of closure, describing the move as a clear demonstration of Oman’s strong confidence in Somalia. The minister thanked the Omani government for its continued support for the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Somalia. A Relationship Rebuilt on Mutual Respect The reopening of Oman’s embassy is the culmination of a steady warming of relations that has accelerated over the past two years. In April 2026, Minister Abdisalam visited Muscat for high-level talks with Omani officials, including a meeting with Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, who reaffirmed Oman’s firm position in support of Somalia’s unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and its non-recognition of any entities outside the framework of the Somali state, as reported in Oman’s Foreign Ministry . During that visit, the Somali delegation also engaged with the Oman Investment Authority to discuss opportunities in energy, infrastructure, logistics, food security, and information technology. The two sides explored ways to activate public-private partnerships and open new avenues for economic integration, as detailed in the Oman News Agency . Economic cooperation has been a central pillar of the relationship. In December 2025, Somali business leaders held a strategic forum with Oman’s Minister of Commerce, Industry, and Investment Promotion, Qais Mohammed Al-Yousef, who noted that bilateral trade volume was around $20 million and “poised for significant growth.” Oman has also expressed interest in investing in Somalia’s Al-Ula Special Economic Zone, with the Omani Authority for Investment Promotion and Export Development offering technical expertise and training to zone management staff, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Muscat talks . What the Embassy Reopening Means The closure of Oman’s embassy in Mogadishu for 36 years was a product of Somalia’s long civil war and the resulting collapse of diplomatic infrastructure in the capital. Its reopening signals that Muscat views the current federal government as a stable and reliable partner, and that it is prepared to invest diplomatic resources in the relationship. For Somalia, the reopening is a diplomatic victory. It adds another Arab and Gulf state to the list of countries with a physical diplomatic presence in Mogadishu, reinforcing the federal government’s claim to be the legitimate and effective representative of the Somali state. It also provides a direct channel for consular services, trade facilitation, and people-to-people exchanges that had previously been handled through third countries. The timing is also significant. It comes as Somalia navigates complex regional dynamics, including the Red Sea security crisis, the Ethiopia-Eritrea standoff, and the ongoing debate over Somaliland’s status. Oman’s explicit rejection of “any entities outside the framework of the Somali state” is a reaffirmation of the international consensus on Somalia’s territorial integrity, and a signal that Muscat will not follow the path of Israel. Critical Note The reopening of Oman’s embassy and the accreditation of a new ambassador are tangible diplomatic achievements, and the Somali government is right to celebrate them. A physical embassy in Mogadishu is more than a symbol. It is an operational platform for trade, investment, and political engagement that did not exist before. But the relationship’s future will depend on whether the economic promises translate into action. The $20 million trade volume is modest for two countries with historic ties and geographic proximity. Oman’s interest in the Al-Ula Special Economic Zone is welcome, but expressions of interest are not investments. The embassy’s reopening creates the conditions for deeper engagement. It does not guarantee that the engagement will materialize. For Somalia, the lesson of the past two years is that diplomatic momentum must be sustained. The visits, the agreements, and the reopening of embassies are necessary steps, but they are not ends in themselves. The test of the Oman relationship will be whether Omani investment arrives, whether trade grows, and whether the embassy becomes a hub of activity rather than a quiet diplomatic outpost. The credentials ceremony on Saturday was a beginning. The work starts now. football.content: اللاعب الدولي الموريتاني أحمد أحمد ينضم إلى الهلال السوداني بعقد يمتد خمس سنوات | وكالة الوئام الوطني للأنباء الموريتانية الرئيسية آخر الأخبار حدث وتعليق تقارير أنباء دولية حوادث ومجتمع مقالات مقابلات ثقافة و رياضة اتصل بنا Français اللاعب الدولي الموريتاني أحمد أحمد ينضم إلى الهلال السوداني بعقد يمتد خمس سنوات أعلن نادي الهلال السوداني تعاقده مع المهاجم الدولي الموريتاني أحمد المختار أحمد، المعروف باسم «أحمد أحمد»، قادما من نادي أفسي نواذيبو، بموجب عقد يمتد لخمس سنوات، في خطوة جديدة ضمن مسيرة اللاعب الشاب الاحترافية. وذكر موقع «Pan Africa Football»، في تقرير نشره يوم 20 أكتوبر الجاري، أن النادي السوداني حسم صفقة ضم المهاجم الموريتاني البالغ من العمر 22 عاما، بهدف تعزيز خياراته الهجومية خلال الاستحقاقات المقبلة. ويعد انتقال أحمد أحمد إلى الهلال محطة مهمة في مسيرته، بعد بروزه مع نادي أفسي نواذيبو، الذي انتقل إليه قادما من نادي تفرغ زينة، قبل أن يلفت الأنظار ويصل إلى المنتخب الوطني الأول. وخاض اللاعب، بحسب التقرير، سبع مباريات بقميص المنتخب الموريتاني، سجل خلالها هدفا، وهو ما يجعله من الأسماء الشابة التي يعول عليها في تعزيز الحضور الموريتاني في الملاعب الإفريقية. ويأتي هذا الانتقال في وقت يستعد فيه الهلال لمواصلة مشواره في دوري أبطال إفريقيا، بعدما حقق الفوز على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بهدفين دون مقابل في ذهاب الدور التمهيدي الثاني، على أن تقام مباراة الإياب يوم 25 أكتوبر الجاري. ويمنح الانضمام إلى ناد بحجم الهلال اللاعب الموريتاني فرصة لاكتساب خبرة تنافسية إضافية، والاحتكاك بمستويات عالية من المنافسة القارية، بما قد ينعكس إيجابا على حضوره مع المنتخب الوطني. سبت, 24/10/2026 - الهلال إلى التصنيف الأول، فيكمل فريق من التصنيف الثالث الرباعي، سواء أسيك ميموزا حال تأهله أو مولودية الجزائر الذي تأهل رسميًا. أما التصنيف الثالث فيضم بالترتيب: أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري، ومولودية الجزائر، وأورلاندو بايرتس الجنوب أفريقي، ومازيمبي الكونغولي، ويتوقف شكله النهائي على تأهل أسيك على حساب المغرب الفاسي، وتأهل مازيمبي على حساب الأفريقي التونسي، ففي حال خروج أي منهما أو خروج أي فريق من
